Medicine.title: Intismeran Autogene plus Pembrolizumab for Resected Stage IIB to IV Melanoma
Medicine.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intismeran autogene (intismeran) is an individualized neoantigen therapy that is designed to induce new T-cell responses and expand preexisting T-cell responses against patient-specific tumor neoantigens, which may potentially improve the efficacy of adjuvant therapy in patients with melanoma. METHODS: In this phase 3, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned patients with completely resected stage IIB to IV cutaneous melanoma in a 2:1 ratio to receive intramuscular intismeran (at a dose of 1 mg) or placebo every 3 weeks for nine doses; all the patients received intravenous pembrolizumab (at a dose of 400 mg) every 6 weeks for nine cycles. The primary end point was investigator-determined recurrence-free survival, assessed in a time-to-event analysis. Key secondary end points included investigator-determined distant-metastasis-free survival (assessed in a time-to-event…

Medicine.title: Breathlessness mechanisms, measurement, and management in adults: evidence update on behalf of The Dyspnoea Society
Medicine.abstract: Breathlessness affects an estimated 40% of adults living with chronic disease, with substantial consequences for individuals, carers, and health-care systems. This Dyspnoea Society Research Statement, developed for researchers, clinicians, and adults living with or caring for someone with breathlessness, provides a state-of-the-art synthesis of recent advances in chronic breathlessness mechanisms, measurement, and management, and outlines a research agenda for the next decade. Key advancements include establishment of neural respiratory drive as a mechanistic contributor to exertional breathlessness; neuroimaging evidence that breathlessness arises from integration of peripheral and central processes within a dynamic brain network involving sensorimotor and cognitive-affective regions, supporting behavioural and psychosocial interventions; and improved measurement through responsive…

Medicine.title: Reframing disease elimination: an update from the Lancet Commission on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Medicine.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with increasing global burden driven by population growth and ageing, persistent harmful exposures, and substantial health inequities. The Lancet Commission on COPD articulated an ambitious vision for disease elimination with prevention, early detection, and intervention. This Review revisits that vision, assesses progress since 2022, and calls for a broader commitment to lifelong lung health as an update of the Commission. Across seven sections, this Review advances a unified framework integrating the biology of lung development and ageing, precision medicine, patient-centred outcomes, and regulatory reform. COPD is not a single, uniform disease; rather, a biologically complex condition shaped by genetic, developmental, environmental, infectious, and behavioural factors across…

Medicine.title: Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity
Medicine.abstract: BACKGROUND: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for the treatment of painful knee osteoarthritis in persons with obesity. METHODS: In two phase 3 trials, adults without diabetes who had painful knee osteoarthritis and a body-mass index of at least 27 were randomly assigned to receive once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide (9 or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-4 and 4, 9, or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-1-OA) or placebo. In TRIUMPH-4, the primary end points were the change in the WOMAC pain score (range, 0 to 10, with higher scores indicating worse pain) and the percent change in body weight at week 68. In TRIUMPH-1-OA, the primary end point was the change in the WOMAC pain score at week 80. For non-pain-related end points, intercurrent events were handled with a treatment-policy strategy. For pain-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was…

Medicine.title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease
Medicine.abstract: BACKGROUND: The inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 is hypothesized to be a therapeutic target for patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Whether neutralizing interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab, a monoclonal antibody, reduces the risk of adverse cardiovascular events remains unknown. METHODS: We conducted a multinational, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation (defined by a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [CRP] level of ≥2 mg per liter). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ziltivekimab (15 mg once monthly) or placebo. The primary efficacy end point was a 3-point major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE). This composite end point included death from cardiovascular…

Medicine.title: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism after Total Hip or Knee Replacement
Medicine.abstract: BACKGROUND: Studies comparing aspirin with anticoagulants for venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty have had conflicting results. METHODS: In a comparative-effectiveness noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned patients undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty to receive aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days. The composite primary effectiveness outcome (death from any cause or symptomatic VTE) and primary safety outcome (bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction) were evaluated through 6 months in a blinded fashion. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference was 0.69 percentage points. RESULTS: Among 18,883 participants who had undergone randomization, 15,317 (7214 with hip arthroplasty and 8103 with knee…

Medicine.title: Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease
Medicine.abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether discontinuing statin therapy in older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease affects the time to a first cardiovascular event is not well characterized. METHODS: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized, controlled trial that enrolled adults at least 70 years of age who were taking statins for primary prevention. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either discontinue or continue statin therapy and other lipid-lowering therapies. The primary outcome was a composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. The primary analysis assessed noninferiority on the basis of the between-group difference in restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years, with a noninferiority margin of -5.2 weeks. RESULTS: A total of 1880…

Medicine.title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a)
Medicine.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide, reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). However, the effect of pelacarsen on cardiovascular outcomes remains uncertain. METHODS: We conducted an international, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and a lipoprotein(a) level of at least 70 mg per deciliter. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous pelacarsen (80 mg) administered monthly or matching placebo. The primary end point was a major adverse cardiovascular event, defined as a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization. RESULTS: A total of 8350 patients underwent randomization, with 8322 included in the efficacy analysis; 4157 patients were assigned to receive pelacarsen, and 4165 to receive placebo.…

Medicine.title: Hyperaldosteronism Remission after Extended Aldosterone Synthase Inhibition
Medicine.abstract: Among patients with hypertension due to primary aldosteronism, reductions in blood pressure and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio persisted for 2 years after completion of an extended course of aldosterone synthase inhibition.

Medicine.title: A Liver-Targeted CIDEB siRNA in Adults with MASLD
Medicine.abstract: A single dose of an siRNA targeting liver expression of CIDEB was associated with a reduction in liver fat of 58 to 80% at week 36 after treatment in persons with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease.

Chemistry.title: Inverse Design of Inorganic Compounds with Generative AI
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry,…

Chemistry.title: Ambipolar Electrochemical Doping of CsPbBr 3 Nanocrystals
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Electronic doping underpins many semiconductor applications but has remained elusive for lead halide perovskite nanocrystals because their high density and low formation energy of defects easily compensate introduced dopants. Here, we use electrochemical doping as a strategy to avoid doping compensation. Electrochemical injection of electrons or holes into the nanocrystal is compensated by surface-adsorbed electrolyte counterions, therefore not compromising crystal structure. We accomplished ambipolar (n- and p-type) doped CsPbBr3 nanocrystals with charge carrier concentrations ranging from intrinsic up to 4.8 × 1017 cm–3 (corresponding to 0.25 charges per nanocrystal). We show that electrochemical doping is reversible and stable at these free carrier concentrations. The extent of doping and stability are enabled by the use of lecithin, a zwitterionic ligand that strongly binds to the…

Chemistry.title: Optical Access to a Molecular Nuclear-Spin Register in Catalytically Relevant Palladium(I) Complexes
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Paramagnetic metal complexes are powerful tools in chemical catalysis and, increasingly, quantum information science, positioning them as ideal tools for quantum sensing within reactions themselves. However, this application requires an interface between spins and light in chemically relevant platforms. Here, we demonstrate that circularly polarized light can generate electron spin coherence in low-symmetry, catalytically relevant Pd(I) complexes. By measuring ultrafast changes in optical polarization with time-resolved Faraday rotation, we optically detect coherent superhyperfine interaction between the Pd(I)-centered electron spin and adjacent 31P nuclei from the ligand at ambient temperature in solution. The electronic origins of this behavior are attributed to excited-state orbital angular momentum through combined spectroscopic and computational analysis, and the optically…

Chemistry.title: Porphyrin-Driven Redox Tuning in Structurally Defined De Novo Heme Proteins
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Designing redox proteins with predictable and tunable electron transfer properties is a major goal in de novo bioenergetics. Here we show that replacing heme B with a series of structurally conservative non-natural metalloporphyrins enables broad modulation of redox potentials over 400 mV in the de novo designed monoheme m4D2 and diheme 4D2 T19D. The non-natural porphyrins bind with high affinity and do not compromise either the heme binding site or global protein structure, as evidenced by X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy. We also report the native-like NMR structure of m4D2 loaded with the non-natural and symmetric iron 2,4-dimethyldeuteroporphyrin IX, confirming our modular approach to tetrahelical redox protein design. This work establishes a versatile platform for constructing tunable electron carriers for engineered bioenergetic pathways and bioelectronic applications.

Chemistry.title: Design and Evolution of an Orthogonal HaloTag for Multiplexed Labeling in Cells
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: The self-labeling protein HaloTag is used to install a wide variety of functional small molecules in cells and living organisms with exquisite specificity with respect to cell type and subcellular localization. HaloTag is a core part of many biotechnology-based tools for sensing, tracking, and manipulating biological systems with a high degree of spatial and temporal control. Due to the limitations of fluorescent proteins and other self-labeling proteins, most of these tools have historically been restricted to a single channel. In this work, we used structure-guided rational design and directed evolution to produce an orthogonal HaloTag protein called OrthoTag which reacts selectively with a modified chloroalkane substrate. OrthoTag retains many of HaloTag’s superior properties, and reaction rate measurements with purified proteins show OrthoTag and its substrate have 109-fold mutual…

Chemistry.title: Named Reactions under Mechanochemical Conditions: A Critical Survey
Chemistry.abstract: Mechanochemistry has progressed from a niche interest to a core method for solvent-free synthesis, providing sustainable and mechanistically unique alternatives to traditional solution-based chemistry. When controlled impact, shear, or vibrational energy is applied under solvent-free or solvent-lean conditions, reactions are promoted within dynamically renewed interfacial regions, revealing new patterns of selectivity, energy efficiency, and process design. This review surveys the historical development, fundamental principles, and analytical frameworks of mechanochemistry, together with an extensive compilation of named organic reactions conducted under mechanochemical conditions. By comparing mechanochemical reactions with their solution-phase counterparts, this review clarifies how stress-induced activation, microsolvation (η control), and auxiliary-mediated interfaces influence…

Chemistry.title: Cationic Ionomer Coatings Promote Anion Electroreduction: Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Electrolysis technologies represent a promising pathway to valorize abundant feedstocks using renewable electricity. While ionomers serve critical roles as ion conductors and catalyst binders in electrolyzers, their impact on electrochemical transformations of ionic species remains poorly understood compared to extensively studied neutral-molecule conversions like water splitting and CO2 reduction. Herein, we use the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction as a model transformation to investigate the influence of ionomer coatings in anion electroreduction reactions, which face fundamental challenges from electrostatic anion depletion near negatively polarized cathodes and premature desorption of anionic intermediates. We demonstrate that cationic ionomer coatings increase local nitrate concentration up to 10-fold compared to bulk electrolyte due to the interfacial Donnan potential.…

Chemistry.title: Magnetic Resonance Silent Activatable Probe with Massive Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated Fibrogenesis
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Biomarker-specific molecular imaging is vital in precision medicine. However, a fundamental challenge of most molecular imaging methods is the difficulty of distinguishing specific molecular signal from nonspecific signal arising from the distribution of the molecular probe. This is even more pronounced in metabolically active organs such as the kidney and liver where the probe may concentrate prior to elimination. As a result, almost all molecular imaging relies on delayed imaging to achieve specificity, but this constrains clinical throughput and impedes rapid assessment of the diseased organ. Here, we report a magnetic resonance (MR) probe, Fe(II)-IAFP2, which combines 3 drivers of relaxivity enhancement to decouple disease specificity from probe distribution. Fe(II)-IAFP2 is MR-silent in its Fe(II) state, producing negligible MR signal even at high concentrations. In inflammatory,…

Chemistry.title: The Structure of Oleate-Capped CdSe Nanocrystals Determined by DNP-Enhanced Dipolar Dephasing Solid-State NMR Spectroscopy
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs) are of interest due to their tunable electronic and optical properties. However, the atomic-level characterization of surface structures of NCs remains an unresolved challenge. Here, we demonstrate that rotational-echo double-resonance (REDOR) experiments can be used to determine structural models of surfaces of CdSe NCs. An atom-efficient ligand-exchange scheme is demonstrated to introduce partially 13C-enriched oleate ligands onto CdSe NCs and enable 13C-dephased REDOR experiments. DNP-enhanced 13C{77Se}, 77Se{13C}, 13C{111Cd}, and 111Cd{13C} REDOR NMR experiments were performed on the 13C-enriched oleate-capped zinc blende CdSe NCs. Despite the modest isotope abundance of 77Se and 111Cd, DNP-enhanced 13C{77Se} and 13C{111Cd} REDOR NMR experiments show significant dephasing due to dipolar coupling between 13C atoms and multiple 77Se or 111Cd atoms…

Chemistry.title: Unifying Polar and Hydrophobic Models of Ice Recognition by Antifreeze Glycoproteins
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Antifreeze glycoproteins (AFGPs) enable polar organisms to survive at subzero temperatures by inhibiting ice growth through selective association with specific crystallographic planes. However, the molecular basis of this interaction and its remarkable selectivity remain incompletely understood, and both polar and hydrophobic binding models have been proposed. Here, we combine the synthesis of AFGP variants with high-resolution NMR spectroscopy, antifreeze activity measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the molecular determinants of ice recognition. Minimally perturbative chemical modifications, including site-specific deuteration and fluorination, were used to probe the contributions of nonpolar and polar interactions while preserving the characteristic AFGP conformation. The combined structure–activity relationships and computational analyses support an…

Chemistry.title: Efficient Long-Wavelength Through-Space Charge-Transfer Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence in Conformationally Adaptive Emitters without Conformational Locking
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Through-space charge-transfer thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TSCT-TADF) emitters often employ conformationally constrained donor–acceptor architectures to control through-space electronic coupling, particularly for long-wavelength emission. Here, we report conformationally adaptive orange-to-red TSCT-TADF emitters based on an S-shaped donor−π–acceptor−π–donor framework composed of phenoxazine donors, xanthene linkers, and a dibenzo[a,j]phenazine acceptor. Structural and NMR analyses reveal substantial conformational mobility, while systematic conformational searches and excited-state calculations identify thermally accessible conformers with distinct donor–acceptor geometries and excited-state characteristics. Comparative studies with reference compounds and fragment-resolved transition-density analysis show that the xanthene linker primarily acts as a conformational…

Chemistry.title: Conjugate Chiral Carbon Dots for Scalable Asymmetric Photocatalysis in Flow
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Carbon dots (CDs) have emerged as scalable, metal-free photocatalysts, but their use as conjugate organo-photocatalysts for enantioselective chemistry remains unexplored. Here, we covalently anchor a chiral imidazolidinone organocatalyst to amorphous, citric acid-derived CDs, giving a colloidal conjugate that acts as both photosensitizer and enantiodetermining component. This chiral CD material promotes the asymmetric radical α-alkylation of aldehydes in up to 84% yield and 93% e.e. Its semihomogeneous nature enables catalyst recovery by precipitation and reuse over five cycles with only minor loss in yield and e.e. The well-dispersed conjugate is also compatible with continuous photoflow, where Bayesian optimization in only 10 experiments enabled a gram-scale reaction in 80% yield and 91% e.e. This work establishes chiral conjugate CDs as a practical, recoverable platform for…

Chemistry.title: Operando pH Measurements of OER within a Porous Oxygen-Evolving Electrode
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Three-dimensional porous electrodes, such as those in membrane electrode assemblies, are widely employed in electrochemical devices due to their high surface area and achievable current density. The heterogeneous internal structure of the porous electrode microenvironment engenders local concentration gradients owing to mass transport constraints. Localized microenvironments with properties distinct from those of the bulk solution are especially prevalent for electrocatalytic reactions that produce or consume protons, as local basic or acidic environments may significantly influence the energy efficiency and selectivity of proton-coupled electron transfer reactions that are necessary for small-molecule activation. Here, we develop an operando method employing polymer-bound fluorescent sensors (PFS) to directly quantify local pH and the internal proton gradient in a porous electrode for…

Chemistry.title: Electrostatic Presolvation Enables Selectivity in Photoinduced Ligand Exchange
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: Functional group compatibility remains a central challenge in photochemical C–H activation with metal complexes. Strongly donating groups preferentially coordinate to the reactive unsaturated metal and suppress weaker C–H coordination and σ-complex formation required for C–H bond activation. Controlling the initial coordination in photoinduced ligand exchange is therefore one approach to achieving selectivity in bond activation. Here, we resolve the elementary steps of photoinduced CO to acetonitrile ligand substitution for Rh(acac)(CO)2 with femtosecond-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the Rh L3-edge. We directly observe the formation of a hitherto undetected transient acetonitrile C–H σ-complex and its subsequent rearrangement to the thermodynamically favored nitrogen-coordinated solvent complex. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the initial C–H coordination is…

Chemistry.title: A Unified Reactivity Scale Predicts Nonenzymatic Phosphoryl Transfer and Nucleophilic Catalysis in Water
Chemistry.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
Chemistry.abstract: The transfer of phosphoryl groups plays a central role in biochemical energy metabolism. Understanding how such reactions could have occurred before the emergence of enzymes is thus crucial for elucidating the chemical foundations of life. Although the factors governing the mechanisms of phosphoryl transfer in water are well understood, predicting whether a given nucleophile and phosphorylating agent will undergo productive phosphoryl transfer rather than hydrolysis remains difficult, thereby hindering the rational exploration of nonenzymatic phosphorylation reactions. Herein, we establish a quantitative reactivity scale that predicts absolute rate constants for nonenzymatic phosphoryl transfer reactions in water based on a linear free-energy relationship (LFER). Using high-throughput kinetics, we measured 11,520 phosphoryl transfer reactions for 145 unique combinations of nucleophiles…

Economics.title: Systemic Cyber Risk: Linking Measurement, Market Incentives, and Policy
Economics.abstract: Many firms and sectors within the global economy heavily depend on a common set of critical technology products and software services, thereby consolidating risk across a small number of potential failure points. The widespread reliance on a limited set of products and services has given rise to many single points of system vulnerability. Such concentration of risk amplifies the potential fallout from security breaches, especially since attackers have strong incentives to attack such products and services. Despite the abundance of tools available to organizations and consumers for safeguarding their data against loss or compromise, advancements in individual defense measures have been more than counterbalanced by an increased susceptibility to systemic events. In this paper, we apply economic principles to the rising danger of systemic cyber risks. The paper is organized around four…

Economics.title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors
Economics.abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely…

Economics.title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets
Economics.abstract: This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high…

Economics.title: In Praise of the Bayesian Bootstrap
Economics.abstract: The key takeaways from this article will be the following: (i) Anytime you can bootstrap, you should! (ii) Use the Bayesian bootstrap instead of the nonparametric bootstrap. (iii) If the bootstrap distribution looks different from the “theoretical” (usually, normal) distribution, don’t (only) report a point estimate and standard error. (iv) Instead (or in addition), report the bootstrap distribution with a plot if you have space for it or an interval if you don’t. (v) Give the Bayesian bootstrap a Bayesian interpretation. (vi) You can use a bootstrap even with (multiway) clustering.

Economics.title: Private Credit, Balance Sheets, and Financial Stability
Economics.abstract: Private credit has become an important source of business financing, raising questions about financial stability. We examine these questions using comprehensive fund- and asset-level data on private credit funds, the dominant form of private credit. Four facts emerge. First, private credit funds are primarily equity financed, with equity accounting for 65–80 percent of assets, compared with about 10 percent for US banks. Second, they engage in little maturity transformation: Fund lives span eight to twelve years, while underlying loans typically mature within two to four years. Third, portfolios are diversified across industries, geographies, and credit strategies. Fourth, equity investors have earned average net annualized returns of about 10 percent after fees, with equity cushions historically absorbing losses before creditors. These findings suggest that private credit funds do not…

Economics.title: Can Government Support for Innovation Create the Next Silicon Valley?
Economics.abstract: Can government support for innovation create the next Silicon Valley? We examine what public research and development can and cannot do to foster regional knowledge hubs. The historical record suggests that many successful hubs owe their origins partly to serendipity and favorable initial conditions. We then review causal evidence from universities, changes in intellectual property rules, new research institutions, wartime R&D, and the space race. Public R&D can raise local innovation, employment, and income, but the effects are heterogeneous, often modest relative to cost, and may partly reflect the relocation of firms and skilled workers from elsewhere. The evidence suggests a central role for complementary local inputs, including entrepreneurs, risk capital, skilled labor, firms, and institutions. Public R&D can help build a hub, but is unlikely to create one on its own.

Economics.title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
Economics.abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This, in turn, makes general skill firm specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

Economics.title: Trust Violations in Research Universities
Economics.abstract: By nearly twice as much as in any other institution that Gallup tracks, public trust in research universities has fallen over the past decade. The causes are not only external. This essay examines two violations of trust that originate within the academy: research that is driven by political advocacy, and a professoriate whose range of ideological viewpoints has narrowed, especially in the humanities and social sciences. The first subordinates the pursuit of truth to political aims; the second erodes the diversity of perspectives that checks individual biases and lets research correct itself. Both break faith with the arguments originally advanced for tenure and academic freedom. Restoring trust demands a renewed commitment to disinterested inquiry and the cultivation of intellectual pluralism—objectives, both, that are best adopted voluntarily, without state censor or interference,…

Economics.title: The Role of Private Debt in the Financial Ecosystem
Economics.abstract: This paper provides an introduction to the modern private debt market and examines its rapid expansion following the 2007–2009 global financial crisis. Traditionally, economists distinguished between public debt markets and private debt in the form of bank lending. In contemporary markets, however, “private debt” refers to credit originated and held by nonbank financial intermediaries, including private credit funds and business development companies. The paper reviews the key drivers of the sector’s growth; analyzes the distinctive features of private lending arrangements and funding structures; and discusses the implications for traditional banking, financial intermediation, and financial stability. While the sector’s rapid growth and increasing complexity warrant careful monitoring, the paper argues that private debt represents an important and likely durable component of modern…

Economics.title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
Economics.abstract: Foreign aid has become a melting pot of motivations and policies, where differently motivated actors often converge on recommended policies while the similarly motivated diverge. Breaking down the “why” and the “how” can illuminate real tensions and reveal false ones. The “why” asks which problems to tackle and who benefits: the recipient, the donor through economic, political, or soft-power returns, or everyone through global public goods. The “how” asks which strategy most cost-effectively addresses a chosen problem. Evidence is central to the “how”: Use it where it exists, produce it where it does not. In particular, approaches that improve state capacity to use and generate evidence can satisfy multiple objectives: strengthen recipient countries, benefit donors, and provide a global public good of knowledge. Ultimately, the “how” is not a linear process, but rather an iterative one…

Economics.title: The Meritocratic Consensus and Stratification in Higher Education
Economics.abstract: American colleges and universities are highly stratified by pre-college academic achievement, family background, and institutional resources. We study the meritocratic consensus in American higher education: Colleges that high-testing students (who are generally also from high-income families) attend spend dramatically more on instruction than do those that enroll lower-testing students. Stratification by test scores has been largely stable since the 1960s, but the stratification of instructional resources has risen sharply since 1970 at both private and public institutions. Nonacademic admissions criteria like athletics, legacy, and affirmative action are second-order in determining the allocation of students to universities. Potential economic justifications for the positive association of instructional expenditures with student prior achievement—q-complementarity between achievement…

Economics.title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data
Economics.abstract: We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

Economics.title: Optimal Policy Rules in HANK
Economics.abstract: We characterize optimal policy rules in a business-cycle model with nominal rigidities and heterogeneous households. The policymaker has access to two instruments: the short-term nominal rate, and lump-sum transfer payments. A policymaker with a traditional dual mandate that targets aggregates uses the same policy rule as is optimal in the textbook New Keynesian model. We then consider a policymaker with a distributional objective. The optimal policy rule now contains an additional term, reflecting the effects of the policymaker’s instruments on consumption inequality. Since, in our model, monetary policy only has very limited distributional effects, this additional term does not materially change optimal monetary policy. Fiscal stimulus payments, on the other hand, have strongly progressive effects and are thus well-suited to cushion the distributional effects of cyclical fluctuations.

Economics.title: Fertility and Family Leave Policies in Germany: Optimal Policy Design in a Dynamic Framework
Economics.abstract: I develop and estimate a life-cycle discrete-choice model of fertility and female labour supply to study the optimal design of a range of child-related policies. First, I examine two German reforms that introduced wage-contingent parental leave payments and expanded access to low-cost public childcare. I find that both reforms raised completed fertility, with the parental leave reform having a particularly strong impact on highly educated women. Second, I solve for a budget-neutral optimal policy portfolio that maximizes either aggregate welfare or fertility, while ensuring that welfare and fertility do not decline for any education group. I consider four prominent child subsidies as well as the degree of tax jointness. My results show that optimal policy has the potential to increase welfare by 0.5% or fertility by 5.7%. While the solutions are qualitatively similar, they prioritize…

Proximal redox coupling enables oxidation damping for stable water electrolysis
Engineering and technology.abstract: The design of atomically precise catalysts requires strategies that regulate their electronic and structural dynamics under operating conditions. While conventional doping can effectively tune bulk materials, it translates poorly to single-atom catalysts (SACs), in which isolated atoms lack extended coordination and are prone to oxidative instability. Here we design atomically dispersed Ru−O−Cr motifs that enable oxidation damping during acidic oxygen evolution. This buffered redox response is accompanied by bounded and partially reversible changes in the local metal−oxygen coordination environment. An organic semiconductor-based photocatalyst sheet for overall solar-driven water splitting
Engineering and technology.abstract: Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using sunlight offers a route to renewable fuel, but translating this reaction into systems suitable for industrial implementation remains difficult. Photocatalyst sheets can overcome key limitations of common direct water-splitting approaches (photoelectrochemical devices and photocatalyst dispersions), but existing photocatalyst sheets rely on inorganic semiconductor nanoparticles and processing techniques that can be difficult to scale. Engineering and technology.abstract: Robot acceptance is shaped by dynamic, multimodal interactions that influence trust, comfort, and behavioral intentions.

Engineering and technology.title: Autane: An autonomous crane for sustained port operations
Engineering and technology.abstract: Fully automated cranes are revolutionizing modern port operations by addressing labor shortages, improving precision, and enhancing safety. Toward this goal, we present the Autane (autonomous crane) system specifically developed for rubber tire gantry (RTG) cranes handling standardized containers in port yards, enabling autonomous safety-critical container grabbing, transport, and placement with high accuracy, adaptability, and efficiency. Autane overcomes the challenges of safe motion of large-scale cranes with centimeter-level precision requirements, providing long-distance high-precision perception. It uses multisensor fusion, real-time obstacle detection, and simultaneous localization and mapping to perceive the environment, identify container features, and dynamically adjust trajectories. By tightly coupling perception, planning, control, and operation and maintenance, Autane…

Engineering and technology.title: Heavy metal acrobatics: Learning dynamic control for skid-steer loaders
Engineering and technology.abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous…

Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background A higher dietary protein intake is often advocated to preserve fat-free mass during energy restriction-induced weight loss, yet the magnitude of effect in previous meta-analyses is highly variable. Objectives We aimed to determine the effects of a higher dietary protein intake on body composition during energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity, with consideration for exercise, age, and protein difference. Methods We performed a systematic review to identify randomized controlled trials implementing higher or normal protein intakes alongside energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity. Random-effects meta-analyses {mean difference [MD] [95% confidence intervals (CI)]} were performed for changes in fat-free mass and fat mass, respectively. Subgroup meta-analysis and meta-regression were performed to…

Life and practice.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid social progress has transformed the health profile of Chinese children and adolescents, with declining diseases associated with poverty and rising diseases associated with wealth. This study aims to describe national trends in disease transitions and examine their associations with multidimensional provincial development. METHODS: In this retrospective study, we analysed data from the 2000, 2005, 2010, 2014, and 2019 waves of the nationwide, repeated, cross-sectional Chinese National Surveys on Students' Constitution and Health in Han Chinese children and adolescents aged 7-18 years from 30 provinces in mainland China. The survey used a multistage, stratified, cluster-sampling design with balanced distributions by age, sex, and residence (urban vs rural). Collected data were prevalences of diseases associated with wealth and development (overweight and obesity, dental…

Life and practice.title: Participatory Budgeting in Public Health: Promise, Evidence, Challenges, and Opportunities
Life and practice.abstract: Participatory budgeting (PB) is a deliberative decision-making process that invites community participation to direct spending for a defined portion of public budgets. Originating in Brazil in the 1980s, PB has since diffused across the globe, including several hundred cases in the United States and Canada alone. PB programs vary but are generally characterized by five core principles: voice, vote, social inclusion, social justice, and oversight. Research on PB shows promising though moderate associations with improved population health outcomes, including infant mortality reductions and health and sanitation spending increases. Despite PB's conceptual alignment with many public health values, adoption of PB by US public health agencies remains limited, constrained by categorical funding requirements, small discretionary budgets, and a polarized sociopolitical environment. This article…

Life and practice.title: Tackling the Commercial Determinants of Obesity: A Review of Key Policies and Strategies
Life and practice.abstract: A growing body of evidence demonstrates that commercial entities play an important role in shaping the prevalence, incidence, and distribution of obesity. This narrative review examines policy solutions to address the commercial determinants of obesity. We describe how five business sectors (food, beverages, and agriculture; media and entertainment; sports and recreation; transportation; and medical care and pharmaceuticals) shape obesity prevalence through three key behavioral pathways: diet, physical activity, and use of medical care. We then examine four categories of tools available to national and subnational governments to address the commercial determinants: legal and regulatory measures, fiscal policies, market governance mechanisms, and litigation. Finally, we discuss three strategies that can support the successful implementation of these measures: building cross-sectoral…

Life and practice.title: Labor Unions and Better Health
Life and practice.abstract: Social-class inequities in health arise from power imbalances in our political-economic system. However, through labor-union organizing, workers can build power to improve their life chances and health. In our review, we describe the rich historical, theoretical, and mechanistic evidence linking unions and health and critically evaluate the state of quantitative research on the topic. Most individual-level and ecological studies have estimated small beneficial or null union-health associations. However, as we describe, the studies are limited in number, particularly outside the Global North, and face many technical and conceptual challenges, including feedback loops between unions and societies' political-economic contexts. We conclude with recommendations for enhancing the rigor and utility of union-health research, including by richly contextualizing studies' findings and by…

Life and practice.title: Nutrition in abrupt sunlight reduction scenarios: a scenario-based modeling study of malnutrition prevention in low-income regions
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background Abrupt sunlight reduction scenarios (ASRSs), triggered by nuclear war, volcanic eruption, or asteroid strike, risk global agricultural collapse. Despite resilient food interventions, economic inequality may leave low-income countries (LICs) at severe risk of malnutrition even where global food production is partially maintained. Objectives To assess the nutritional adequacy of low-cost ASRS-resilient food baskets (~$1/person/d) for LIC populations across 2 postdisaster periods, and to identify micronutrient gaps requiring targeted intervention. Methods A scenario-based nutritional modeling study was conducted. Food baskets were constructed for 2 periods: Period 1 (≤1 y postdisaster), based on conventional crop stocks and offal, and Period 2 (years 2–3), incorporating single-cell protein, lignocellulosic sugar, seaweed, and wheat flour. Nutritional adequacy was assessed…

Life and practice.title: Impact of supplementation with fortified balanced energy–protein during pregnancy on birth outcomes: a community-based randomized trial among pregnant females in southern Nepal
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background The World Health Organization recommends balanced energy–protein (BEP) dietary supplementation in undernourished populations to reduce risk of stillbirth and small-for-gestational age (SGA), but variation in the composition of interventions has hindered scientific consensus. Objectives To assess the effect of daily fortified BEP supplementation during pregnancy on SGA birth and secondary birth outcomes. Methods MINT (Maternal Infant Nutrition Trial) was a 2 × 2 factorial, household randomized, unblinded, efficacy trial to assess the effect of a daily fortified BEP supplement during pregnancy and/or lactation compared with no supplement on birth and infant growth outcomes in Sarlahi, Nepal. This analysis examines the effect of pregnancy supplementation on the primary outcome of SGA (<10th centile), among live-born infants with birth weight measured <72 h of delivery and…

Life and practice.title: (R)-1,3-butanediol (S)-lactate ester improves insulin sensitivity, modulates appetite hormones, and reduces urea excretion: a randomized controlled crossover trial in adults with obesity
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background Lactate and ketone bodies, such as (R)-β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB), are central to metabolic regulation, serving as important energy intermediates and signaling molecules. The molecule (R)-1,3-butanediol (S)-lactate ester (LaKe) is a new supplement that offers dual supplementation of lactate and βHB. Objectives This study aims to evaluate whether 28 d of LaKe supplementation followed by acute dosing would 1 ) improve insulin sensitivity and 2 ) influence appetite-regulating hormones, gastric emptying, substrate metabolism, and body weight. Methods In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, 10 adults (males = 5, females = 5) with obesity consumed 25 mL (27.75 g) LaKe or noncaloric placebo twice daily for 28 d. Fasting blood and anthropometric measurements were obtained after each intervention period. Participants then ingested an additional dose of the…

Life and practice.title: Riboflavin status in pregnancy and its association with hemoglobin and anemia risk: cross-sectional findings from the OptiPREG study
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background Anemia in pregnancy poses a serious health problem for females globally. In addition to iron deficiency, the most common nutritional cause of anemia, a deficiency of riboflavin (required for iron metabolism) may also be implicated, but this has rarely been investigated. Objectives This study investigated the association of riboflavin status with hemoglobin (Hb) concentrations and anemia risk during pregnancy. Additionally, we provide preliminary data on the effect of riboflavin supplementation on Hb. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of data from the Optimal Nutrition in Pregnancy using a Personalized Approach (OptiPREG) study. The participants were healthy pregnant females ( n = 2002) from Ireland and Northern Ireland (United Kingdom), sampled at the 12th gestational week (GW). In a subsample ( n = 134), we additionally analyzed postintervention data (36th GW)…

Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: To systematically evaluate associations between multidimensional sleep parameters and non-invasive cardiac autonomic nervous system metrics derived from heart rate variability (HRV) in patients with obstructive sleep apnea, and to identify the autonomic pathways most closely linked to sleep disturbances. METHODS: Using overnight polysomnography from the Shanghai Sleep Health Study cohort, a three-stage dimensionality-reduction strategy compressed 147 sleep parameters and 68 HRV metrics into 59 parameters (5 functional domains) and 25 metrics (5 autonomic domains). For each sleep-HRV pair, multivariable linear regression was adjusted for age, sex, BMI, blood pressure, fasting glucose, and lipids. Life and practice.title: Poor Test–Retest Stability of Nocturnal REM Sleep Onset Markers in Narcolepsy Type 1
Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: To assess the test-retest stability of nocturnal sleep-onset REM periods (nSOREMPs) in untreated patients with narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), and of nocturnal direct REM (nDREM) transitions and their clinical and biological correlates. METHODS: We included consecutive children and adults with NT1 diagnosed according to ICSD-3-TR criteria based on excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) findings, or CSF hypocretin-1 deficiency, without using nSOREMPs for diagnosis. All patients underwent two untreated overnight polysomnographic (PSG). nSOREMP was defined as REM sleep within 15 minutes of sleep onset, and nDREM as direct transition from wakefulness or N1 to REM sleep without intervening N2 or N3 sleep. Life and practice.title: Data-driven thresholds for annualized changes in body mass index and waist circumference and all-cause mortality in United States adults aged 65 years or older: a secondary analysis of a prospective cohort
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background Although longitudinal changes in body mass index [BMI (in kg/m 2 )] provide prognostic value beyond single measurements, and waist circumference (WC) adds complementary information about abdominal size, standardized annualized percentage change (APC) thresholds for mortality risk remain unestablished. Objectives To identify data-driven BMI and WC APC thresholds associated with all-cause mortality in United States adults aged ≥65 y. Methods This secondary analysis utilized National Health and Aging Trends Study Rounds 1-14 data (2011‒2024). A common analytic framework was applied within BMI ( n = 5321; 2010 deaths) and WC ( n = 5375; 2082 deaths), respectively, to identify candidate thresholds using training samples (80%) via the Contal and O’Quigley methods. Sensitivity analyses evaluated sex-specific, alternative follow-up horizons, unintentional weight loss, and final…

Life and practice.title: Respiratory self-similarity is a sleep apnea endotype that predicts cardiovascular disease related mortality
Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: Pathological respiratory chemoreflex activation (high loop gain) in sleep apnea may activate the carotid body and induce excessive sympathetic nerve output, and independently add to the risk of adverse outcomes. This study aims to determine whether a high loop gain of the respiratory control system during sleep, estimated by respiratory self-similarity (SS) and the algorithm-derived central respiratory event index (CREI), is associated with new-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD-related mortality. METHODS: A secondary analysis of The Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) and Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). High SS% and CREI were defined as the highest quartile. Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: To define physiologically interpretable visual biomarkers of progressive sleepiness during 48-hour total sleep deprivation and determine whether pupillary and cortical visual measures detect changes not captured by brief behavioral or resting cardiovascular assessments. METHODS: Twenty-four healthy adults completed one rested baseline assessment and eight supervised deprivation sessions across 48 hours of continuous wakefulness. Business.title: "If we don't act now, someone will die" : temporal riskwork in action
Business.abstract: In this ethnographic study, we develop the concept of temporal riskwork -- actions taken to alter the temporal dynamics of risk -- by examining how riskworkers navigated situations of multiple dynamically evolving risks under severe time constraints. In such contexts, decisions about how and when to act are critically interdependent and made with attention to assessing urgencies, priorities and volatility of risk. Our study revealed how risk can present both synchronic and diachronic competing temporal demands, requiring temporally complex riskwork. We studied a mental health crisis team where actors collectively responded to clients’ urgent, often accelerating risks in high-stakes, time-pressured environments. We contribute to the literature by developing a model of temporal riskwork that explains how actors can collectively manage a set of ongoing risks by engaging in two connected…

Business.title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
Business.abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Business.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
Business.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth…

Business.title: Private debt versus bank debt in corporate borrowing
Business.abstract: Using administrative bank loan-level data matched to private debt deals, we study the interaction between private and bank debt for a large segment of dual borrowers. These firms use private debt for investment and bank credit lines for liquidity insurance. Private debt carries higher spreads and commonly features flexible, equity-like terms that are associated with greater reliance on bank credit lines. Relative to bank-only borrowers, dual borrowers obtain more and larger credit lines and draw them more intensively following liquidity shocks. Our findings suggest that private debt substitutes for bank term loans but complements banks’ provision of credit lines.

Business.title: Shadow banks on the rise: Evidence across market segments
Business.abstract: This paper examines the comparative advantages of shadow banks across market segments. Combining credit bureau data on retail loans in India with weather shocks as a proxy for credit demand, we show that Fintechs respond more in uncollateralized markets. In contrast, non-Fintech shadow banks exhibit stronger responsiveness in collateralized markets. Exploiting geographic heterogeneity in the adoption of digital payments, we identify technology as the key advantage for Fintechs. Leveraging four natural experiments, we document the significance of lower regulation for non-Fintech shadow banks. Our results suggest that the comparative advantage of shadow banks differs across market segments.

Business.title: Benefiting from Culture Wars: Resource Mobilization in Polarized Issue Domains
Business.abstract: Organizations engaging with contested social issues may struggle to mobilize resources due to disapproval from hostile audiences. Yet, some may benefit from increased support from sympathetic audiences, leaving unclear when such support will outweigh opposition. We propose that variation in audience reactions depends partly on how contestation is structured. We theorize that ideological polarization—the extent to which opposing stances on an issue sort along ideological lines—may enhance resource mobilization in contested issue domains. As polarization increases, contested issues pit opposing identities against each other and heighten threats to sympathetic audiences’ worldviews. New ventures in more polarized domains may attract greater support as sympathetic audiences respond by investing in aligned ventures, a mechanism we term “compensatory investment.” This relationship…

Business.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
Business.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by…

Business.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
Business.abstract: We quantify the short-term impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on sales performance through a series of large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading crossborder online retail platform. Over 2023–2024, the platform integrated GenAI into seven business workflows spanning customer service, consumer-product matching, advertising, and seller services. We find that GenAI adoption increases sales in most workflows, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3% depending on GenAI’s marginal contribution relative to baseline firm practices. Across the four GenAI applications with positive sales effects, the implied annual incremental value is roughly $5 per consumer—an economically meaningful impact given the retailer’s scale and the early stage of GenAI adoption. Business.title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
Business.abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and…

Business.title: Looking the Part? How Candidates’ Race and Attire Shape Employers’ Hiring Decisions in a Low-Wage Labor Market
Business.abstract: Racial disparities in employment persist in the United States, particularly in low-wage labor markets in which employers frequently cite self-presentation, especially attire, as a basis for hiring decisions. Yet, whether improving professional attire yields equal returns across racial groups remains largely unexamined. Drawing on status characteristics theory, we argue that professional attire functions as an ambiguous proxy for unobservable traits such as motivation and reliability, making it susceptible to racialized interpretations. We predict that professional attire will yield weaker hiring returns for Black candidates than for their White counterparts and that perceived professionalism mediates this gap. We test these arguments using data from a gig-staffing platform comprising over 1 million job applications with profile photos, supplemented by a preregistered experiment that…

Business.title: Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
Business.abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Business.title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
Business.abstract: We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

Business.title: The role of financial markets in the unraveling of credit
Business.abstract: We investigate how long an insolvent debtor can avoid default when survival benefits creditors collectively, but individual creditors gain from early repayment. Standard theory predicts that debt is not rolled over and default is immediate. Previous experimental studies of related environments suggest that liquidation is delayed, and we confirm that pattern here. We then study how secondary markets affect outcomes. The duration of the credit pool is unaffected, but average net payoffs increase because claims are held longer before redemption. With markets, realized payoff dispersion is significantly higher. Prices do not predict liquidation timing but correlate with realized payoffs.

Business.title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
Business.abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. Business.title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
Business.abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum…

Computer science.title: The commutativity problem for effective varieties of formal series, and applications
Computer science.abstract: A formal series in noncommuting variables Σ over the rationals is a mapping \(\Sigma ^* \rightarrow {\mathbb {Q}} \) from the free monoid generated by Σ to the rationals. We say that it is commutative if the output does not depend on the order of the symbols in the input. The commutativity problem for a class of series takes as input a (finite presentation of) a series from the class and amounts to establishing whether it is commutative. This is a very natural, albeit nontrivial problem, which has not been considered before from an algorithmic perspective. We show that commutativity is decidable for all classes of series that constitute a so-called effective prevariety , a notion generalising Reutenauer’s varieties of formal series. Computer science.title: Synergizing LLMs and Formal Methods for Neural-Symbolic Reasoning
Computer science.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding, generation, and reasoning, but their outputs remain probabilistic and error-prone. Formal methods (FM), by contrast, provide mathematically rigorous reasoning, but suffer from limited accessibility. This article explores a neural-symbolic paradigm that unifies these complementary strengths and presents case studies that illustrate how LLMs can lower the entry barrier to formal methods while the latter provide reliability, interpretability, and guarantees absent in purely neural AI models. We argue that synergizing LLMs with formal methods is a promising direction for building AI systems that are not only powerful but also trustworthy by construction.

Computer science.title: Reasoning Beyond Prediction: From Data-Driven to Causal Software Engineering
Computer science.abstract: Software engineering is an intellectually demanding, creative discipline that juggles a web of interdependent tasks to design, build, and assure the quality of increasingly complex systems. As our expectations from software soar—with demands spanning AI-driven products, pervasively distributed and cloud-native architectures, and deeply embedded cyber-physical environments—its complexity steadily increases. In response, a new wave of co-engineering methods and tools, fueled by deep learning, has emerged to augment the process, enhancing automation and decision support. Yet, these advances remain far from delivering the kind of intelligent support that modern software development demands. We call for a new paradigm of human-machine cooperation—one where machines don’t just automate routine tasks or predict from learned patterns, but actively amplify engineers’ reasoning through the lens…

Computer science.title: An Ethics Ecosystem for AI
Computer science.abstract: This article diagnoses ethical failures associated with AI as resulting from the lack of a robust ethics ecosystem . Drawing on the domain of health and healthcare, we identify the components of a functioning ecosystem and explain how an ecosystemic approach helps to manage the scale of the ethical challenges in the domain of AI relative to more typical alternatives.

Psychology.title: Older yet faster: Representational development explains accelerated semantic processing in older adults.
Psychology.abstract: Slower responses in older age are often taken as evidence for cognitive decline, yet they may also stem from representational changes shaped by lifelong learning. Building on the information-accumulation perspective on aging, we argue that behavioral change across the lifespan can arise from representational systems continuously updated through learning from the environment. This view predicts that aging may bring both benefits and costs: Performance improves when task demands are congruent with accumulated knowledge but declines when they conflict. We provide convergent evidence for this account across three studies, each comprising the following components. First, in tasks requiring participants to access word meanings (i.e., when task demands were congruent with representation), we found that older adults (70-80 years old) exhibited faster semantic processing speed than younger…

Psychology.title: Self-esteem and social relationships: A meta-analytic review of longitudinal studies with continuous time modeling.
Psychology.abstract: This preregistered systematic review investigated reciprocal effects between people's self-esteem and the quality of their social relationships by meta-analyzing the available longitudinal data. Analyses were based on 82 samples, including 86,850 participants. Mean age of samples ranged from 8 to 63 years. We used continuous time modeling to account for between-study differences in the time intervals between assessments, which ranged from 1 week to 6 years. Psychology.title: Long-term development of a motor memory
Psychology.abstract: Human behaviour is developed through continuous adaptation to our environment over a range of timescales. Extensive studies have investigated the mechanisms and computations underlying this process of sensorimotor adaptation using several hundred trials. However, most of our motor skills have had countless hours of practice. Here we study a simple motor adaptation task using thousands of training trials over multiple weeks to study the long-term development of a motor memory, and examine changes in adaptation, retention, interlimb transfer, decay, spontaneous recovery and generalization. Unlike previous studies, participants showed near complete compensation to the novel dynamics, along with long-term increases in retention and spontaneous recovery. Psychology.title: A natural field experiment on the effectiveness of economic sanctions before and after the Russian invasion of Ukraine
Psychology.abstract: Here, using two rounds of natural field experiments based on an audit-study approach, we investigated whether sanctioned Russian government officials retain access to the international financial system. Researchers sent 7,081 email solicitations to intermediary firms in 202 countries and jurisdictions to establish shell companies and set up corporate bank accounts. Responses to sanctioned names (middle initial modified) are compared with equivalent solicitations from non-sanctioned placebo names. Round 1 results in December 2020 reveal no statistically significant difference in financial access for the sanctioned names compared with placebo. Humanities and arts.title: Bias Against Boltzmann Brains?
Humanities and arts.abstract: A popular indifference principle for self‐locating probability faces skeptical challenges, most notably a skeptical challenge concerning Boltzmann Brains. We examine the prospects for various views that prescribe some degree of bias in place of indifference. Although a bias view has attractive anti‐skeptical features, it turns out that bias leads to puzzles about deference to chance, reflection, and other related principles.

Humanities and arts.title: Refusing International Debt and the Postcolonial Politics of Yentua in 1970s Ghana
Humanities and arts.abstract: In 1972 the government of Ghana refused to repay loans contracted on the international debt market. As a pivotal moment in the history of decolonization, the policy of Yentua, or ‘We Shall Not Pay’, marked an unprecedented move in Ghana’s relationship with its foreign creditors. Eight years of debt negotiations had exposed the persistence not only of Western financial economic and political control, but also of debt as a mechanism to assert neocolonial power. At the same time, negotiations opened up the possibility of challenging creditors and the continuing relationships of dependency, violence, and extraction. While across Africa the 1970s were marked by increasing economic uncertainty and militarism, this situation did not diminish the will of the Ghanaian public to reimagine the emancipatory potential of debt repudiation. Humanities and arts.title: Solving the Dual Puzzles of Collective Harm
Humanities and arts.abstract: Suppose some uncoordinated group of agents causes tremendous harm, but none of the individuals could have meaningfully changed this result by acting differently. These “collective harm” cases have been the subject of extended philosophical discussion, but this paper argues that there are really two different, if connected, puzzles presented by such cases: (1) a puzzle about how to characterize the moral injury to those who suffer this harm (the “wrongness puzzle”) and (2) a puzzle about why agents may do something wrong in participating in producing this harm (the “participation puzzle”). This paper elaborates these puzzles, defends the idea that they are different from each other, and offers solutions to them both. Humanities and arts.title: Higher‐Order Tense Realism
Humanities and arts.abstract: Realism about tense comes in various forms. In “Tense and Reality” (2005) and “The Reality of Tense” (2006), Kit Fine offered a helpful taxonomy that contributed to shape the current debate on the topic. In our paper “Eternal Facts in an Ageing Universe” (2012), we improved upon this taxonomy, identifying a further type of view that Fine leaves out: Dynamic Absolutism. Both these taxonomies construe the different versions of tense realism in terms of first‐order quantification over facts or states of affairs. Our goal is to show that the logical space of these first‐order tense‐realist positions can be replicated using higher‐order quantification instead. Humanities and arts.title: What Is Time?
Humanities and arts.abstract: We argue that time is the great enabler: it is that which makes causation and change possible. We develop this idea into a functionalist account of time that has some very nice features: (i) it differentiates time from space where needed, (ii) it illuminates time via its connection to causation and change, (iii) it accounts for the apparent multiple realizability of time, and (iv) it correctly classifies worlds that have time as such. We compare our account to three rivals: time as the great necessitator, time as the great informer, and time as the measure of change. We show that treating time as an enabler does better.

Humanities and arts.title: Substitutional Quantification and Arithmetical Truth
Humanities and arts.abstract: In the mid‐20th century, there was a debate about whether the quantifiers in first‐order logic should be understood objectually or substitutionally. This debate typically focused on ontology and assumed that we could use only one of these two types of quantification. After Kripke and others influentially argued that the two kinds of quantification were logically equivalent, defenses of substitutional quantification were rare. Following Gottlieb and Field, I argue that Kripke was wrong and that substitutional consequence is language‐bound and non‐compact. While of no help with ontology, I also argue that so‐understood, substitutional quantification can be applied to help explain our grasp of a determinate notion of arithmetical truth. Society and law.title: The Seeds of State Capture: Merit and Patrimonialism in the Colonial Bureaucracy
Society and law.abstract: Bureaucracies vary in the extent to which hiring is meritocratic versus patrimonial. Such outcomes are typically seen as the result of politicians’ behavior. However, politicians often delegate hiring to existing bureaucrats. When political leaders are socially distant from communities they seek to govern and these areas are peripheral to politicians’ core interests, bureaucrats’ private preferences can dominate hiring decisions instead. Colonial and other forms of external state-building typify cases where patrimonialism created by bureaucrats, not politicians, can emerge. Digitizing individual-level records across six decades of British rule in Ghana, we find evidence of patrimonialism rather than meritocracy in the hiring of African staff, with large inequities across ethnic groups. Society and law.title: The Influence of Police Unions in Local Elections: Evidence from U.S. Cities’ Spending and Performance
Society and law.abstract: Despite growing attention to local policies governing public safety issues, and mounting reports of police union spending to local candidates, the role of police unions in local politics remains understudied. We address this gap by assembling a novel, large-scale dataset on campaign finance in U.S. mayoral elections, covering 2,303 races across 1,073 cities from 2001 to 2019. We document that police unions frequently donate to mayoral candidates—especially in mid-sized and large cities—targeting likely winners and incumbents, and without displaying clear partisan bias.
